title: Per-client SLA Priority Batcher — proposal and experiments
body:
Context and motivation:

This doc proposes a scheduling primitive and a set of experiments for a per-client-SLA priority tier layered on top of the existing continuous batching runtime. Goal: allow customers with explicit SLA tiers (e.g., paid gold/silver/free) to get latency and tail guarantees while preserving high GPU utilization through continuous token-level batching.

Why new behavior is needed:
- Current token-level continuous batching optimizes throughput and average cost, but can starve small high-priority requests when long-running low-priority requests are continuously coalesced into large microbatches.
- Request-level fairness (simple round-robin or strict queue order) wastes batching opportunities and increases cost significantly for high-throughput workloads.
- We need an approach that gives quantifiable latency guarantees per SLA class while retaining much of token batching efficiency and leveraging KV cache locality when possible.

Design overview (high level):
- Define SLA classes: GOLD / SILVER / BRONZE (configurable per-customer). Each SLA class maps to a priority weight and a soft latency SLO target (e.g., p95).
- Introduce a small-time-budget preemption window at token-aggregation time: when constructing a microbatch, the scheduler reserves a small fraction of batch slots (configurable) as fast-path slots for high-priority requests that arrive shortly before dispatch.
- Two-tier accounting: (1) token credits accrued per SLA over a sliding 1s window, used to determine immediate admission to fast-path slots; (2) request credits for per-request headroom to avoid being bisected across many microbatches.
- Precedence: within a dispatch cycle, prioritize GOLD requests into fast-path slots until their token-credit budget is exhausted, then SILVER and so on. Unused reserved slots fall back to general batching to preserve utilization.

Key mechanisms and rationale:
1) Token-credit bucket per-SLA
- Each SLA has a replenishing token-credit bucket that grows at a configured rate (tokens/sec) proportional to purchased throughput or configured SLA weight.
- Admission to the fast-path requires the request's token length <= available credits. If not enough credits, request joins the general token-coalescing queue.
- Rationale: credits provide a smooth, tunable knob to trade strictness of priority vs utilization.

2) Fast-path reservation window (microseconds to low-milliseconds)
- When a dispatcher prepares a dispatch, it opens a short window (configurable; starting experiments at 1.5ms) to collect high-priority arrivals for reserved slots.
- This window is short enough not to materially increase p50/p95 for fast-path requests but long enough to capture frequent arrivals in high-throughput scenarios.

3) Request-bloat protection
- Some requests have many tokens; admitting a single long request into a reserved fast-path slot could defeat the goal. Introduce per-request headroom accounting: limit the maximum admitted token length to a fraction of the fast-path slot budget or require long requests to burn more credits proportional to length.

4) KV cache affinity and kernel selection
- Prefer admitting requests into the same dispatch as other requests that share prefix or KV cache state to increase cache hits and reduce total latency.
- Kernel selection hints: fast-path microbatches should prefer execution kernels optimized for short sequences and minimal launch overhead (e.g., fused attention path with low overhead).

5) Graceful fallback and fairness enforcement
- If a high-priority request cannot be admitted within a configured latency bound, it should fallback to an accelerated retry path (e.g., dedicated small-slot dispatch) rather than permanently block lower-priority traffic.
- Periodic fairness correction: every N seconds, the scheduler compares realized service (tokens served, p95) vs entitlement and temporarily biases admission to under-served SLAs until balance restored.

APIs and config knobs (runtime and tenant-facing):
- SLA profile: weight, tokens_per_sec, burst_capacity_tokens, target_p95_ms, fallback_policy (queue | retry-dedicated-dispatch).
- Scheduler-level knobs: fast_path_window_ms, reserved_slot_fraction, max_fast_path_token_length, fairness_correction_interval_s, correction_intensity (scale factor).

Metrics to collect (mandatory for experiments):
- Per-SLA: p50, p95, p99 latency (end-to-end), tokens_served, avg_batch_utilization, kv_cache_hit_rate, number_of_preemptions, admission_ratio_fastpath.
- System: GPU occupancy, average microbatch_size_tokens, microbatch dispatch latency, percent of reserved_slots_used.

Tradeoffs and failure modes:
- Over-reserving reduces utilization; under-reserving leads to SLA misses. The credit model helps smooth the extremes but requires per-tenant tuning.
- Long-tail requests can distort credit accounting; headroom and proportional burn mitigations are necessary.
- KV cache locality heuristics may increase p95 for some SLAs if they prefer coalescing by prefix over strict priority; need to expose policies (strong affinity vs strict priority).

Simulation and experimental plan (short-term milestones):
- 0: Baseline replay of production request traces on current continuous batcher to get p50/p95 per tenant and microbatch stats.
- 1: Implement a simulator that supports reserved-slot windows and token-credit accounting. Run parameter sweep over fast_path_window_ms={0.5,1.5,3}, reserved_slot_fraction={0.05,0.1,0.2}, tokens_per_sec multipliers.
- 2: Select 3 production-like mixes: (A) many small requests heavy throughput, (B) mixed lengths with a few long streaming requests, (C) bursty arrival patterns from enterprise customers. Measure utilization and SLA compliance.
- 3: Paper-prototype in staging: lightweight scheduler plugin that can be toggled per-AZ. Collect real traces, compare to simulator.
- 4: Gradual canary rollout: route 5% of GOLD traffic through plugin and monitor metrics + automated rollback thresholds.

Open questions and TODOs:
- Credit replenishment formula: should token credits be linear with weight or follow a convex function to better protect gold customers during bursts? Experimentation required.
- How to bill for fast-path usage? Counted as same-per-token billable unit but flagged in billing logs so sales can audit overuse. Need alignment with product/pricing.
- Interaction with Dedicated pools: should reserved fast-path enforcement be applied inside dedicated pools or only in shared multi-tenant hosts? Expected answer: both, but different defaults.
- KV cache eviction: when fast-path inflates working set for a tenant, should we prioritize pinning its KV pages (memory pressure tradeoff)? Investigate small LRU-with-reservation policy.

Implementation notes and rough data structures:
- Lightweight per-SLA in-memory struct: {credits, last_tick, weight, burst_capacity, reserved_slots_in_use}.
- Dispatcher flow (simplified):
  * snapshot arriving requests into waiting queues (segmented by SLA and approximate token_length)
  * open fast-path timer -> collect candidates -> admit up to reserved slots using credit checks and headroom checks
  * fill remaining slots with general coalescing algorithm (existing token-level packer)
  * mark KV affinity hints for kernel selection layer

Observability and debugging guidance:
- Expose per-dispatch debug traces that annotate why a request was admitted into fast-path or deferred (credit insufficient, headroom, or affinity mismatch).
- Add lightweight per-tenant admission logs (sampled at 1/1000) for invoices and postmortems.

Acceptance criteria for rollout:
- For GOLD tenants in canary, p95 latency improves or stays equal while overall GPU utilization degradation <= 7% vs baseline.
- For SILVER tenants, p95 within defined SLA band (configurable) and no more than 10% regression in tokens_served per minute.
- No customer-visible error increases (4xx/5xx) attributable to scheduler change.

Notes to reviewers / discussion items:
- I intentionally kept fast_path_window_ms small to reduce the risk of increasing tail latency; reviewers with empirical evidence for a different default please call it out.
- Product needs to weigh in on billing semantics and customer-configurable defaults. Eng-PS should budget time for customer on-boarding playbooks.

Appendix: quick sketch of an experiment outputs table we expect from simulator:
- scenario, reserved_fraction, window_ms, gold_p95_ms, silver_p95_ms, utilization_pct, kv_hit_rate
- A,0.1,1.5,84,180,73,0.62
- B,0.1,1.5,92,210,68,0.71

End of proposal.

- [Sofia] draft product note on SLA config and billing (due 2024-12-15)

Other references and reading:
- See existing continuous batching experiments in /serving-runtime (tokenized-flow arbiter, mini-window allocator) — this approach is complementary and must be validated against those options.
- Past discussion thread: slack #serving-runtime: "priority-batcher-proposal"

Unresolved: where to persist per-tenant credit state for multi-node scheduling coherency (local fast-path is simpler but could cause cross-node unfairness). Options: centralized credit service, gossip protocol, or conservative local budgeting. Need experiments and SRE input.
